extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, state regulators, FERC/RTO/ISO staff, and electric utilities (policy and legal teams)
extracted.subtask_description: Stakeholder comments addressing EPA's proposed Section 111(d) Clean Power Plan: legal limits of EPA authority, state plan design, reliability protections, conversions of rate- to-mass-based goals, compliance mechanisms, and permissible measures. Provides specific recommendations and principles EPA should adopt in any final emission guideline and state-implementation framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a dynamic reliability safety valve
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must adopt a dynamic reliability safety valve that provides the States the flexibility they need to ensure reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Mercury and Air Toxics Rule's one-year reliability safety valve as precedent; safety valve should allow utilities to seek implementation delays without enforcement risk. It should be able to address multi-state reliability issues and involve FERC, NERC, RTOs/ISOs and regional planning entities in open and transparent processes to certify that plans will not harm bulk electric system reliability. Static, one-time reviews are inadequate; ongoing assessments are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit States to stage implementation past 2030 for reliability and RUL
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should permit States to stage the implementation of the rule out past 2030 as necessary to recognize reliability and the remaining useful lives (RUL) of existing EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should be allowed to extend timelines to avoid forced retirements or reliability compromises; solicit FERC/Transmission Operator input to avoid SIPs that undermine bulk electric system reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety valve must be ongoing and allow SIP adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: A safety valve applied only at SIP drafting/approval is unlikely to preserve reliability; EPA must allow States to adjust SIPs dynamically in response to unforeseen changes in the electric grid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because compliance depends on dynamic, system-wide factors (market rules, outages, storms, technology, economic growth), EPA should permit rolling RSV processes to reassess prospective multi-state reliability at multiple points before and during implementation and to provide compliance/enforcement flexibility while long-term solutions are developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize interdependence of grid factors when defining BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: By defining the 'best system of emissions reductions' to encompass the whole electric system, EPA makes compliance dependent on changing, interdependent factors beyond States' control; EPA must account for this in allowing flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States ought to consider availability, dispatchability, and emissions impacts, but EPA must permit dynamic amendments so States are not forced to choose between compliance and reliability, economic growth, or technological innovation. Examples include plant parasitic loads, NRC regulation changes, generator breakdowns (e.g., SONGS), pipeline outages, transmission congestion, market economics and load growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate-to-mass conversion methods must be guidance, not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s proposed methods for converting rate-based CO2 goals to mass-based equivalents can only serve as guidance to States and cannot be binding requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory EPA-selected methodology would usurp States' authorities under Section 111(d) to establish performance standards. The notice's language about achieving 'equivalent in stringency' should not be interpreted to preclude State-chosen methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA's proposed rate-to-mass methods are inconsistent/arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed conversion methods employ presumptions opposite those used to determine rate-based goals, producing arbitrary results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The straightforward, consistent approach is to use the product of the goal-computed MWhs (denominator) and the goal-calculated CO2 rate/MWh. EPA's backing out of non-CO2 MWhs in the mass conversion improperly lowers tonnage results relative to the rate computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA cannot mandate tonnage limits for new fossil-fired sources under 111(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot regulate new sources as existing sources under Section 111(d); mandating tonnage limits on new fossil-fuel sources as part of a Section 111(d) plan is unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New-source regulation belongs in the new-source standard framework; 111(d) plans should not include tonnage limits binding on new sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust state or utility performance goals for unanticipated exceedances without penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where actual emissions exceed the performance goal due to unanticipated circumstances (economic conditions, severe weather, postponed retirements), the State or utility performance goal should be adjusted accordingly with no penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exceedances are modest and not due to intervening factors, no corrective measures should be required so long as the State is reasonably close to its goal. This principle should govern milestone and emission performance checks under alternative 5-year approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA lacks authority to reestablish subsequent BSERs or performance goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111 does not permit EPA to establish a subsequent BSER or to reissue performance goals for existing sources that have already undergone the section 111(d) process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's reliance on the eight-year review in section 111(b) to re-issue NSPS for existing units is misplaced; EPA cannot force existing sources to go through reissuance of standards as if they were new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-implementation emission checks are the only permissible out-year mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: For out-year issues (after 2027/2025), the only legally permissible measures are post-implementation emission checks and, where appropriate, state readjusted plans, not mandatory second plan re-submittals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals should be adjusted for unforeseen circumstances. EPA should not require a second state plan submittal as a default mechanism to maintain performance beyond initial plan implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trading or emissions averaging cannot be considered BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Trading or emissions averaging approaches should not be considered the BSER because BSER must derive from reductions attainable 'inside the fence' at the affected source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After setting performance standards, affected utilities may, with State approval, use flexible compliance options (averaging, offsets, trading), but States should not be required to achieve reductions exceeding aggregation of individual EGU obligations, nor should EGUs be obligated to achieve reductions beyond individual obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not combine steam EGU and NGCC source categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The two existing categories for affected EGUs (steam EGUs and NGCC units) should remain separate; categories are defined by engineering design and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA opposes combining categories as a legal prerequisite for identifying re-dispatch between categories as BSER or for facilitating averaging/trading that includes both categories. BSER cannot legally include trading or dispatch between units.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA 111(d) authority limited to inside-the-fence measures (enforcement scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's authority under Section 111 is limited to defining BSER that can be implemented 'inside the fence line' at each source—technological and operational measures that improve source emissions per unit of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no legal basis to require state plans to include additional enforceable measures applying to a diverse range of non-EGU entities beyond affected EGUs; enforceability considerations under different plan approaches should reflect this limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Section 110(k)(3) and (4) approval mechanisms is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may use partial approval/partial disapproval and conditional approval mechanisms under CAA Section 110(k)(3) and (4) for complete state plans, and these options should be part of plan approval mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA supports the broadest possible approval mechanisms to allow full or partial plan approvals while preserving flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-rate improvement (HRI) projects should be exempt from NSR as routine maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must make clear that heat-rate improvement projects undertaken to comply with existing source emission guidelines are exempt from New Source Review (NSR) as routine maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given EPA's history of NSR enforcement and the risk of retroactive NSR prosecution, states and sources need assurance that HRI actions won't trigger NSR; otherwise economic harm, stranded assets, and premature unit closures could result. If HRI actions trigger NSR as determined by the State, those additional costs should be included in compliance cost assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance standards should not be tied to state historic data
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing performance standards should be unrelated to state historic data; EPA must establish BSER and emission standards by considering cost, non-air and environmental impacts, and energy requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States must be granted flexibility in establishing goals, including adjustments for unforeseen circumstances and consideration of remaining useful life of designated facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: States should determine which plants reduce generation under building block 2
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to building block 2's alternate procedures, States should have the discretion to determine which plants would decrease generation as NGCC generation is increased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should not prescribe a required ordering (e.g., decrease coal-fired first then oil/gas steam) that maximizes reductions; plant-level dispatch and local circumstances should guide decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA should not penalize States for failing to capture theoretical multi-state cost savings
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA lacks expertise to properly assess cost savings associated with multi-state approaches and should not penalize States or use hypothetical multi-state savings to gauge reasonableness of state-specific goal costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State cost reasonableness should be judged on actual state circumstances; theoretical multi-state benefits should not be used to make state goals more stringent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-year alternative (2025 goals) are unachievable and should not be strengthened
rubrics_metrics.description: The five-year alternative building block goals (2025 final goals after a 2020-2024 phase-in) are unachievable in many States due to flawed assumptions underlying each building block and therefore cannot be rationally strengthened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should not assume building blocks can be achieved rapidly without undermining reliability or imposing unreasonable costs; implementation timelines must be feasible given planning and infrastructure lead times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow credit for other CO2-mitigation measures but do not require them as BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures such as T&D efficiency improvements, partial CCS retrofits, biomass co-firing, and new NGCC units that mitigate CO2 should be eligible for credit toward goal achievement, but should not be mandatory components of BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should be able to include such measures in plans and receive credit, but EPA must not treat them as required elements of BAER/BSER determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new NGCC emissions should be left to State discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether emissions from a new NGCC that displaces existing generation are counted toward affected EGU performance should be decided by individual States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including new NGCC emissions in 111(d) plans may be appropriate in States with high electricity growth or where the statewide goal exceeds the NGCC NSPS; in other contexts it may be counterintuitive. States should have discretion to include or exclude new NGCC emissions in compliance demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: States may credit emissions differences exceeding new-source NSPS toward 111(d) goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Where new fossil-fuel-fired EGU emissions performance exceeds the NSPS, the emission difference should, at the States' prerogative, be credited toward the State's required Section 111(d) goal and allowed as a compliance option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-level discretion should govern whether such credits are included in compliance demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional EPA guidance should be advisory, not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Any additional technical resources or guidance EPA provides to States should be advisory in nature and not mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA would welcome guidance, including on multi-state plan development, but it must not be binding or displace State authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow crediting for reductions concurrent with or prior to plan base period
rubrics_metrics.description: States should be able to appropriately credit CO2 mitigation activities that occur concurrent with or backdated before the plan toward state goal accomplishment or to adjust state goals accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance determinations historically have not relied on single historic dates; crediting concurrent or prior reductions is consistent with state flexibility and the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for crediting RE and demand-side EE in rate-based plans
rubrics_metrics.description: RE and demand-side EE in a rate-based approach may be credited either via MWh crediting/adjustment applied to affected EGUs' reported CO2 emission rates or via an adjustment based on estimated CO2 emissions avoided for the power pool/region; approach selection should reflect sound accounting and State discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MWh crediting approach assumes avoided emissions come directly from particular affected EGUs; an alternative is region/power-pool based adjustment estimating avoided emissions. States should have flexibility to choose the most appropriate mechanism consistent with accurate accounting.
